name: AWS Step Functions
summary: AWS’s serverless workflow engine: state machines in JSON that call AWS services directly.
intro: A Step Functions state machine is a JSON document written in the Amazon States Language. Task states do work, Choice states branch, Wait states pause, Parallel and Map states fan out, and any Task can declare `Retry` and `Catch` rules. A Task can call more than 14,000 API actions across over 220 AWS services through SDK integrations, or any HTTPS API, so many workflows need no glue code at all. Data passed between states is shaped with JSONata expressions or the older JSONPath fields.

You pick one of two types when you create the state machine. Standard workflows run for up to a year, run each step exactly once, keep 90 days of execution history, and are billed per state transition. They can also wait for a job to finish (`.sync`) or for a callback carrying a task token, and their Distributed Map runs up to 10,000 child executions in parallel. Express workflows run for at most five minutes at much higher rates, at least once (asynchronous) or at most once (synchronous), and are billed by executions, duration and memory.
strengths: No workers or servers: AWS runs the engine and every step
Calls DynamoDB, SQS, ECS, Glue and hundreds of other services directly, without a Lambda in between
The console draws each execution as a graph, with every step’s input and output kept for audit
Standard workflows’ exactly-once steps suit non-idempotent work such as payments
limits: Each state’s input or output is capped at 256 KiB, so large data must go through S3
A Standard execution’s history is capped at 25,000 events; long loops must hand off to new executions
Logic lives in a JSON DSL that’s harder to test and refactor than code, and it only runs on AWS
Per-transition billing makes busy Standard workflows expensive; high-volume work belongs in Express
Step Functions Local, the downloadable emulator, is now unsupported; AWS points to the `TestState` API for testing state logic

snippet.title: Charge with retries, then wait three days (JSONata)

story: Amazon had wrestled with multi-step processes for years. Jeff Barr wrote in 2012 that he’d been told a single Amazon.com order “needed to make its way through at least 40 different states or steps before it was considered complete.” AWS’s first answer for customers was the Simple Workflow Service (SWF), launched in February 2012, in which you wrote “decider” programs that polled for events and chose the next step. It was powerful, but by the later account of the team that built it, developers found it complex.

Serverless functions made the need sharper, because a real application meant coordinating many small functions and services, with retries and error handling between them. On December 1, 2016 AWS launched Step Functions: you declare the workflow as a state machine in JSON, the Amazon States Language, and AWS runs it and draws it. Tim Bray, who edited the States Language specification, introduced it as a “Serverless Distributed Cloud Microservices Polyglot Workflow Orchestration Coordinator thingie.”

Since then Step Functions has learned to call AWS services directly, first a handful and from 2021 almost the whole AWS SDK, so many workflows need no glue functions at all. It has also added cheaper Express workflows, Distributed Map for very large parallel jobs, and JSONata for shaping data.

choices.choice: Workflows as declarative JSON, not code
choices.why: A States Language document can be validated, drawn as a graph and run by AWS with no customer code for the control flow. The price is a DSL that’s harder to test and refactor than a program, the opposite trade-off to Temporal’s.

choices.choice: Retries and error handling declared per state
choices.why: `Retry` and `Catch` rules put failure handling in the workflow definition, so each function can stay small and unaware of what happens around it.
At launch AWS charged $0.025 per 1,000 state transitions, which suits long, low-volume business processes. High-volume event processing got the cheaper Express type in 2019.

choices.choice: Call AWS APIs straight from a Task
choices.why: Direct service integrations, and later SDK integrations addressed by ARN, removed the Lambda functions early workflows needed just to call DynamoDB or SQS.

timeline.text: Amazon SWF, its predecessor, launches in February
Step Functions launches at re:Invent on December 1
Express workflows for high-volume, short runs
SDK integrations reach over 200 AWS services; Workflow Studio
Distributed Map for large parallel jobs
Preview of an AI agent reasoning step (AgentCore)
